title: The Tyranny of Low Expectations
author: Foundation Father
summary: Writing as a father preparing his son for a rite of passage, the author argues that high expectations are a form of trust and low expectations a quiet form of abandonment. After laying out what his son must do to pass the rite, he saw the boy shift from intimidation to a better attitude, simply because he had been told the task was hard but doable and that his father would be alongside him. Children sense what is expected of them and respond accordingly, so low expectations cut them off before they try. They are also easy on the father, since they require no attention or accountability. The piece links high standards to discipline, noting that clear standards must exist before discipline can be fair, and it ends with a stark claim about fathers who never discipline.
points: High expectations communicate trust and give a child weight and steadiness, while low expectations communicate the opposite.
Low expectations are easy on the father because they spare him effort and accountability, which makes them a form of abdication.
Clearly communicated standards are the precondition for fair discipline; without them enforcement is arbitrary.
Expectations work best when paired with presence: the father sets a hard task and commits to doing it alongside his son.
quotes: High expectations = high trust. That trust you instill in them gives them weight and helps steady their steps.
Children can sense when you have low expectations for them, and they will respond accordingly.
Low expectations cut your children off at the knees before they even try to jump. The problem is that low expectations are so easy, not only on the child, but also on the father.
It is so easy to expect their room to stay messy, or expect them to forget their chores, or to expect them to play video games all day.
Low expectations require no effort on your part. They are a form of abdication.
In the first place, there must be standards, clearly communicated, in order to fairly administer discipline. Otherwise, enforcement is arbitrary.
He still wasn’t excited. But something had changed. At dinner that night, he spoke about everything he needed to do to “be a man.
